11545-travels-in-the-united-states-of-am:
William Priest, a musician late of the theatres of Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Boston, published his travels in London in 1802. The book covers 1793 to 1797, with journals of two Atlantic voyages added. He wrote the work on his return in 1797 for friends, and resisted publishing it for years.

He feared, with a joke, that a preface might only put readers to sleep, and that his book would not much affect the price of opium. The volume mixes travel notes with songs and poems, among them verses on a shepherd who leaves the forest for native shades and is welcomed back by Indians. It gives a theatre man's view of the young republic.
12694-history-of-the-american-clock-busi:
Chauncey Jerome wrote this 1860 memoir-history of the American clock trade from his own long career in Connecticut. He traces the shift from wooden works, made slowly by a few men with plain tools, to brass movements turned out by large factories. Exports, southern markets, and the panic of 1837 all shape the story.

Jerome names makers, firms, and rivals, and tells how firms rose and fell, some closing after making thousands of clocks a year. P. T. Barnum's link to the Yankee clock trade gets its own section. The book stands as a rare insider account of how a small-state craft grew into a national industry.
14761-caxton-s-book-of-curtesye:
William Caxton's Book of Curtesye, first printed at Westminster about 1477, teaches good manners to young people entering service in a great household. Edited by Frederick J. Furnivall for the Early English Text Society, this reprint sets Caxton's text beside two manuscript copies from Oriel and Balliol colleges.

The treatise covers how to stand, speak, eat and serve without giving offence, and how to show respect to lords, ladies and fellow servants. Its rules now sound quaint, but they reveal a whole social order: rank, cleanliness, speech and table conduct as moral training. For readers of early English, the old spelling and notes make it both a conduct book and a language record.
16747-a-canadian-manor-and-its-seigneurs:
George M. Wrong, a history teacher at the University of Toronto, wrote this 1908 tale of one Canadian manor across a hundred years, 1761 to 1861. It starts with the founding of Malbaie, its first seigneurs, its burning by the British in 1759, and the Highland seigneurs who followed. Pictures and maps help place the land.

Wrong follows lords, tenants, priests, and soldiers as French rule gives way to British rule and a new Canada takes shape. The manor stands for a whole social order: land, rank, church, and kin, tested by war and change. The book gives a clear, local view of big history, told through one place and the folk who held it.
16804-an-eye-for-an-eye:
Anthony Trollope wrote this 1879 novel in two volumes, of love, promise, and ruin in Ireland and England. Fred Neville makes a promise, is called home to Scroope, and faces the Earl in trouble, while scenes shift from Ennis and Liscannor to Ardkill and the cliffs. The tale opens with a lady long shut in a private asylum in the west of England.

Trollope weighs a young man's word against his rank, his kin, and his own weak will. The lady's fixed, brooding mind haunts the whole book, a grim price for broken faith. Readers who like Trollope's moral tales will find a darker, shorter novel than his Barset books, with his usual sharp eye for class and conscience.
17164-narrative-of-a-mission-to-central-:
James Richardson's mission to Central Africa in 1850 and 1851, published in 1853 after his death, tells a British trek from Tripoli toward Lake Chad. An editor shaped Richardson's eight small journals, dispatches, and notes into this narrative. Caravan lists, camel drivers, interpreters, and trade in slaves and goods fill the early chapters, with desert marches and talks at Mourzuk and Ghat.

Richardson aimed to push lawful trade and end slave traffic, and his journal records both hope and hardship on the road. The tone is that of a field report, keen on places, prices, and peoples met. Readers of African exploration will find a frank, detailed record of a mission cut short by its leader's death.
18544-narrative-of-a-mission-to-central-:
James Richardson wrote this account of a British mission to Central Africa in 1850 and 1851, printed at London in 1853 as its second volume. Sent at government expense, the party traveled through the Sahara fringe toward Bornu, meeting sultans, traders, and desert peoples. Chapters note palaces and huts, markets, charms, meteors, and the politics of local rulers.

Fellow travelers Dr. Barth and Dr. Overweg appear often, with Barth setting out for Aghadez and news of his route reaching the camp. Richardson records vocabularies, trade in salt and agates, and the spread of Islam with a traveler's curiosity. The book remains a rich source on the Sudan before later colonial rule.
26372-panther-eye:
Roy J. Snell's Panther Eye, issued by Reilly and Lee at Chicago in 1921, is a boys' mystery set among gold mines and northern trails. It opens in inky darkness inside a mine, where Johnny Thompson learns that Frank Langlois is dead. His guide, a man called Pant, leads him forward with sure steps past mine props, though their torch has died.

Chapters promise a fight in the night, Chukche treachery, the big cat, the mystery of Mine Number One, and three men vanished. Later come a Russian dagger, a girl called Cio-Cio-San, a city of gold, a kidnapping, and machine-gun fire. A Vladivostok thread, with reindeer and stolen gold, drives the chase. The book mixes mine danger, treachery, and boyish pluck.
30145-pathfinders-of-the-great-plains-a-:
Lawrence J. Burpee chronicles La Vérendrye and his sons as pathfinders of the great plains, in a Toronto and Glasgow volume from 1914. Early service and a first attempt at exploration lead across the plains to the Mandan Indians, then to the discovery of the Rocky Mountains and La Vérendrye's latter days. A map of explorations from 1731 to 1743 by Bartholomew opens the book, with a bibliographical note and index to close.

Pictures show an Indian encampment by Paul Kane, an Assiniboine Indian by Edmund Morris, Mandan girls, and a tablet deposited by La Vérendrye in 1743. Burpee writes popular history in the Brook series manner, clear and brisk, for readers who want the French explorers of the Canadian west without a heavy scholarly apparatus. The volume stands as a readable record of a hard, brave search.
33772-hawk-eye:
David Cory, author of Little Indian, writes a boys' adventure of Native American life in this 1938 Grosset and Dunlap book. It has a signature page from Joseph K. Dixon, leader of the Rodman Wanamaker historical expeditions to the North American Indian. Chapters open with wild geese, plans and pelts, loading the canoes, and jealous Slow Dog. Illustrations show shafts speeding to their marks while two birds flutter and fall, and Hawk Eye with a rabbit.

The story follows a young hero through hunting, canoe travel, camp life, and rivalry, in the tradition of Cory's Indian stories for children. Cory writes with respect for Native skill, courage, and community, and with attention to outdoor detail. Young readers and collectors of classic boys' books will enjoy a straightforward, warm-hearted adventure from a popular author of the period.
35196-gwen-wynn-a-romance-of-the-wye:
Gwen Wynn is a tale of the Wye by Captain Mayne Reid, in a form dated eighteen seventy-seven. The name page calls it a love tale of that stream. The first part is named for its lead girl. It opens with a guest who floats down that stream past a town to a wreck abbey.

Past the banks he may spy a small tent like house on the grounds of a gents home. Tall poplars on a long isle hide it as he draws past. That isle is an old bed of the stream, left dry past long ages of shift. The off shoot runs slow and bent, past a cliff of old red stone. Gloss leaves of far shrubs mix with home holly and ivy past the brow of that cliff. That lush reach sets the scene.
41004-an-eye-for-an-eye:
An Eye for an Eye, by William Le Queux, opens in a train of the Underground Railway in London. Chapter one is called The Mystery Man. Two men talk in low tones of a find made days past, a secret held by them alone. One holds that two strange affairs link as one.

His friend, Richard Cleugh, will not buy the claim without hard proof. Cleugh is a sharp young reporter for the Comet, a bright evening paper. He gets out at Blackfriars, in the murk of a line not yet lit by power, and dives into the crowd of City men. The teller calls the chain a romance of love, guile, and great sins. He vows a startling truth will come out in time. Mystery fans get a London tale of linked crimes and a slow hunt for proof.
422-the-romany-rye:
George Borrow continues his wandering tale in this sequel to Lavengro, opening in a damp dingle at dawn. The narrator, camped with gypsies, mends a chaise wheel, tends his forge, and talks with Belle, Isopel Berners, and other road folk. Gypsy lore, horse deals, and sharp talk fill the roadside days.

Borrow mixes travel, language study, and picaresque jest, with long talks on books, faith, and fair play. The Romany Rye of the title names both the road and its free spirit. The book charms as a rambling portrait of England seen from the campfire, not the coach.
43677-whispers-at-dawn-or-the-eye:
Whispers at Dawn, or The Eye, a mystery story for boys by Roy Snell, was published in Chicago in 1934 by Reilly and Lee. A note by Snell insists the marvels are real feats of the electrical wizards of the age, fairly recorded. Twenty-five chapters run from Three Black Boxes through Down a Beam of Light and A Human Spider to The Whisperer Talks.

Chapter one brings Johnny Thompson to a brownstone facing the grounds of the Chicago Century of Progress fair. He reaches to ring the bell, and the door opens in silence. A voice bids him step inside, but no face appears. The door shuts behind him with a slow, ominous softness. Snell builds a boys' thriller on early television, photo-cells, and other new electric wonders.
56841-the-disappearing-eye:
Fergus Hume, author of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab and The Green Mummy, wrote this mystery novel, copyrighted by the Dillingham company at New York in 1908. Twenty-two chapters run from A Weird Discovery through The Cipher and The Airship to The Whole Truth, with Gertrude's defence misprinted in the contents out of its place.

Chapter one opens on the road, the narrator Vance twisting his motor car round a corner. Young Cannington, a subaltern, quotes that adventures are to the adventurous, and credits it to a man who wrote it in his sister's album. Vance traces the saying to Beaconsfield in Coningsby and Ixion in Heaven. The talk turns to Marr, the older man Cannington's sister Mabel is taken with. Vance warns that Cannington, the man behind the gun, fires at the seen enemy, while half the firing is at the unseen.
58734-pleasing-poetry-and-pictures-for-t:
S Babcock of New Haven printed this little book of verse and pictures for children in 1849. Its title promises food for both the mind and the eye. A rhyme on the cover sings of a pretty new book that Mary can read, full of verses and pictures. A plate of a bee-hive opens the set.

The first piece is The Little Busy Bee, held up as a model of hard work for young children. It borrows the famed hymn on the bee that improves each shining hour. The child reader is urged to be busy in books, work, or sound play. The Dead Bird follows, with the hard note that what we call sport is too often cruelty to small things.
68722-in-the-twinkling-of-an-eye:
Sydney Watson wrote In the Twinkling of an Eye, copyright 1918, printed at Los Angeles. Watson had written The Mark of the Beast and Wops, the Waif. A foreword by the author heads the book. It opens with a letter he once had from a ladies' temperance committee in a southern town. They had bought his tales for the people in large numbers.

His latest story had sadly undeceived them, the letter ran. In it his hero gave a hurt woman in a lonely place a few drops of brandy from his hunting flask. Had Watson held total abstinence fully at heart, they held, the flask would have held water. The moral lies on the surface, Watson says. Some persons cannot see anything from the side of real, actual life. He writes because the book's standpoint, looking for the Lord's return, will be misunderstood by many earnest people.
69438-tedious-brief-tales-of-granta-and-:
Arthur Gray, master of Jesus College, wrote Tedious Brief Tales of Granta and Gramarye under the name Ingulphus, published at Cambridge in December 1919 with illustrations by E Joyce Shillington Scales. The title quotes A Midsummer Night's Dream on tales merry and tragical, tedious and brief. The tales first appeared in Cambridge magazines.

Contents open with a piece to two Cambridge magicians, then The Everlasting Club and The Treasure of John Badcock. The Necromancer, Brother John's Bequest, and The Burden of Dead Books follow. A frontispiece shows the entrance gateway of Jesus College. Readers get ghostly and antiquarian tales rooted in Cambridge colleges and their old libraries.
70527-the-eagle-s-eye:
William Flynn, lately chief of the United States Secret Service, furnished the facts for a true story of German spies in America, put into novel form by Courtney Ryley Cooper in 1919. The first chapter opens in the German embassy at Washington, beneath a great portrait of Kaiser Wilhelm.

A nervous man there works out a code from an old dictionary, page and word numbers matched to sheets of figures. Chapters go on to plots against the fleet, against labour, and against Canada. Names in the contents include von Rintelen and Robert Fay, and places like Hopewell, Virginia. Flynn's aim was to show how deep the intrigue ran.
74101-the-street-of-the-eye:
The Street of the Eye and nine other tales, by Gerald Bullett, was first published by John Lane the Bodley Head in London in 1923. The contents list the title story first, then Sleeping Beauty, The Enchanted Moment, and The Mole. A Sensitive Man, Miss Lettice, Wedding-Day, Dearth's Farm, and The Ghost follow.

The House at Maadi closes the volume in four parts: an afternoon in April, Sheila Dyrle, Sheila Fairfield, and an evening of the same day. A note records that The Mole appeared in the London Mercury. The title story opens in talk. Stories of the supernatural, says Saunders, serve one useful purpose: they test a man's capacity. Incertitude, a sense of imminent surprise, is the very salt of life. Men, he argues, fit their pigeon holes more easily than the subtle folk suppose.
75195-the-mystery-of-the-peacock-s-eye:
The Mystery of the Peacock's Eye is a detective novel by Brian Flynn, first printed at London in July 1928. Its first chapter is the Hunt Ball at Westhampton. The strains of the Red Ruritanian Band die gently away, and the ball, the outstanding event of the season, has exceeded all past successes.

It was actually honoured, so it was whispered, with the presence of royalty. The contents then bring Mr Bathurst a distinguished visitor, and Chief-Inspector Bannister gets a busman's holiday. A case of identity and John Martin's evidence follow. A room is ransacked at Rest Harrow, and a newspaper and a second suit-case appear. The peacock's eye itself arrives at chapter fourteen. Alan Warburton leads trumps, and Bathurst holds the ace. Flynn's gentleman detective works through county society, where class lines are sharp and struggling against them has little chance of success.
78694-the-humor-of-bill-nye:
The Humor of Bill Nye gathers the comic pieces of the American newspaper humorist who wrote under that name. John W Gunn chose the pieces and wrote the opening essay. The book appeared in 1924 as Little Blue Book number 771, in the cheap series edited by E Haldeman-Julius.

The first piece, Words About Washington, sets the tone. Nye complains that Washington has been wrapped in so much glamour that he looks like a god rather than a tall man with large feet. Boys who want to grow into Washingtons, he says, should know that the Father of his Country was not perfect. Washington could swear at his troops strongly enough to crack the ice in the Delaware a week early. Nye insists he means no disrespect: the flaws make the hero safe to imitate.
79264-idol-s-eye:
Carol Emshwiller's Idol's Eye is introduced by an editor still pleased with her earlier short story, Love Me Again, from the February 1956 Science Fiction Quarterly. Readers, he says, urge the magazine never to let her appear elsewhere.

Philippa, shelling peas on the back steps, hears heavy footsteps come round the house and knows who it is. Through ill-fitting glasses she sees little but her black hair and blurred shapes, yet she is sure of the mockery in his voice when he tells her she is looking pretty. I may not see very well, she answers, but I know I am not pretty. He presses for a kiss, is put off till after the wedding, and warns her he will be boss then.
a-canadian-manor-and-its-seigneurs-the-s: George McKinnon Wrong tells the hundred year story of a Canadian manor and its seigneurs. The history runs from 1761 to 1861 and begins with the founding of Malbaie on the St. Lawrence. Early chapters recall Cartier and Champlain at Malbaie and the first seigneur of the place. Wrong then traces settlement, landholding, and change through a century of Canadian life.
an-eye-for-an-eye: Anthony Trollope writes An Eye for an Eye, a novel in two volumes whose later chapters find Fred Neville making a promise. The story turns on love, honour, and a fatal choice, set between England and Ireland. Trollope's steady, moral prose gives the tragedy its weight, as character drives events toward a hard end.
britannica-1911-abaye: 'Abaye is the headword of a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry names a Babylonian amora, a teacher of the rabbinic tradition, born in the middle of the third century. He died in the year 339, the entry states. No school, book, or saying is set down in the notice. The entry fixes his name, order, and dates for readers of the rabbinic entries. It sends them to the amora article for the setting.
britannica-1911-aye-aye:
Aye-Aye is the accepted name, of uncertain meaning, for the strangest of Madagascar's lemurs, Chiromys madagascariensis. It looks somewhat like a long-haired, dusky cat with very large eyes, a broad round head, and long thin fingers ending in pointed claws.

One finger, the third, is remarkably thin, and the animal uses its claw to pick wood-boring grubs from holes first cut open with strong front teeth. It also feeds on juices, tearing open sugar-cane stalks to reach them. Wholly night-active, it lives alone or in pairs in bamboo forests and builds large ball-like nests of dry leaves in tree forks. Found by Sonnerat in 1780, it long stood in a family of its own before ear structure placed it among the lemurs.
britannica-1911-bird-s-eye:
Bird's-eye is a name shared by several small, bright flowers. What links them is a small spot, or eye, at the flower's centre. The primula is called bird's-eye for its yellow centre, the 1911 Britannica entry says. The adonis carries the same name as pheasant's eye. The blue veronica, or germander speedwell, is a third flower in the group. One word thus covers a look, not a family of plants.

The name spreads beyond flowers in the entry's second half. A sort of tobacco is called bird's-eye, with mottled stalks cut up with the leaves. Bird's-eye maple is a speckled form of maple wood named by likeness. Thackeray's novels mention a bird's-eye handkerchief in the same spirit. The entry is a short word note of a few lines. Its point is how one image, a bright speck like a bird's eye, names many things.
britannica-1911-gilles-de-roye:
Gilles de Roye, also called Egidius de Roya, was a Flemish chronicler who died in 1478. His work is noted in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was likely born at Montdidier and became a monk of the Cistercian order. In time he taught theology in Paris and was abbot of Royaumont, by the Oise river.

About 1458 he retired to the convent of Notre Dame des Dunes, near Furnes, and gave his days to study. There he wrote his chronicle of the dunes, the Annales Belgici. The work sums up and carries on the chronicle of Jean Brandon, a monk who died in 1428. It deals with the history of Flanders, and with events in Germany, Italy, and England, from the year 792 to 1478. The chronicle was printed at Frankfort in 1620, and its first part again at Brussels in 1870.
britannica-1911-golden-eye:
Golden-eye, in the 1911 Britannica, is a name loosely given in Britain to two distinct ducks, from the rich yellow of their eyes. The entry, signed by Alfred Newton, sorts the confusion out. One bird is the tufted duck; the other, the true golden-eye of books, is a diving duck of the genus Clangula.

Linnaeus named the same species twice over, not knowing his two birds differed only in age or sex, and fowlers still split the female Morillon from the adult male. The golden-eye breeds in hollow trees across the northern parts of both hemispheres, and Scandinavians set up nest-boxes on tree trunks, robbing them of eggs and down. The entry describes the male's green-glossed head and white cheek patch, then takes up Barrow's duck of Iceland and the small buffel-headed duck of North America.
britannica-1911-skye:
Skye is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides in Scotland. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica maps its lochs, hills, and shrinking folk. Narrow sounds part it from the mainland on every side. No point inland sits more than five miles from the sea.

Jagged Cuillin peaks rule the view by land or water. Six of them top three thousand feet in height. Red Hills and the weird Storr rocks stand to the north. Names like the Needle and the Prison mark its stone shapes. One dark lake hides under the Cuillin cliffs in gloom. People fell from twenty-three thousand in 1841 to under fourteen thousand in 1901. Most of those left spoke Gaelic, half of them Gaelic alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herve-auguste:
Hervé-Auguste-Étienne-Albans Faye was a French astronomer, born at Saint-Benoît-du-Sault in October 1814 and dead at Paris in 1902. Son of a civil engineer, he entered the École Polytechnique in 1832, left early, and joined the Paris Observatory as a pupil in 1836. There he discovered the periodic comet that bears his name in 1843, winning the Prix Lalande, and he entered the Academy of Sciences in 1847.

Faye taught geodesy at the École Polytechnique, served as rector at Nancy, and held the astronomy chair at the École Polytechnique from 1873 to 1893. He also led the Bureau des Longitudes and served briefly as minister of public instruction in 1877. His fame rests on practical and theoretical work alike, from better methods of measurement and a zenithal collimator to early uses of photography in astronomy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-la-ha:
Jean de La Haye, a French Franciscan Bible scholar born in Paris in 1593 and dead there in 1661. He spent his boyhood in Spain and took the habit in the Alcantarine reform. He lectured in philosophy and divinity, preached with distinction, and from 1620 held high offices in his order and at Louis XIII's court.

De La Haye authored or edited some forty folio volumes. He edited Bernardine of Siena, Francis, and Anthony of Padua, and wrote preaching commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, and Revelation. His monuments are the Biblia Magna of 1643 and the nineteen-volume Biblia Maxima of 1660, both built on the Vulgate with gathered commentaries and variant readings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sieur-de-lave:
Pierre Gaultier de Varennes, Sieur de La Vérendrye, discoverer of the Canadian West, was born at Three Rivers, Quebec, in 1685 and died at Montreal in 1749. His early manhood passed as a soldier of France, and he was wounded at Malplaquet. Returning home, he entered the fur trade. He built three posts west of Lake Superior: Fort Saint Pierre in 1731, Fort Saint Charles in 1732, and Maurepas in 1734.

A sincere Christian, he carried Jesuit chaplains with him, first Father Mesaiger, then Father Aulneau de La Touche. In June 1736 Aulneau left east with La Vérendrye's eldest son and nineteen voyageurs for provisions. The whole party was slain that very day on an island in the Lake of the Woods. He resisted native pressure to avenge the Sioux massacre. His posts' voyageur crews gave rise in time to the Métis people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-mart:
John Martin Moye was a priest of the Diocese of Metz, founder of the Sisters of Divine Providence, and missionary in China. He was born at Cutting in Lorraine on 27 January 1730 and died at Trier on 4 May 1793. Sixth of thirteen children of John Moye and Catharine Demange, he learned his first Latin from an elder brother, a seminarian, and finished his classical studies at Pont-à-Mousson's college.

Next he read philosophy at Strasburg's Jesuit college and joined Metz's theological seminary of St Simon in autumn 1751. Ordained priest on 9 March 1754, he was named vicar in the episcopal city that same month. His great zeal for souls drew attention, and many pious ladies placed themselves under his firm and wise direction. From them he chose select souls to found schools for country children, the seed of his congregation.
caxton-s-book-of-curtesye:
Frederick J. Furnivall edited a fifteenth-century verse treatise on manners for the Early English Text Society, in an edition first issued in 1868. William Caxton had printed the poem at Westminster about 1477-78. Furnivall prints Caxton's text beside two manuscript copies, from Oriel MS. 79 and Balliol MS. 354, so readers can compare readings line by line.

The poem itself instructs a child or young servant in courtesy: rise, wash, and behave at table. Wash your hands so clean that no spot shows on the towel. Leave no spoon standing in your dish. Keep your trencher clean. Stay silent while another speaks. Editorial notes argue over single words with great care, Skeat's views included.
doe-osti-3010923-integration-and-validat:
Cyber physical resilience for power systems is organised as layered mitigation in the RD2C Capstone I roadmap from Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, dated October 2025. Seventeen authors led by Sri Nikhil Gupta Gourisetti and Sumit Pustake Nandanoori set out multi layer strategies for systems whose failures cross between computing and physical plant. The roadmap works at system level rather than device level.

Simulation assets anchor the plan, including HYPERSIM distribution system models and an IEEE 9500 node feeder with GridLAB-D. Testbeds for realistic scale experiments support the modelling. The document frames detection, response, and recovery as coordinated layers for distribution grids under cyber attack.
history-of-the-american-clock-business-f:
Chauncey Jerome wrote this history of the American clock trade, and his own life, in 1860. Jerome says the preface's claim plainly: clocks had grown to a great branch of American industry. Sixty years before, a few men with clumsy tools met the demand. By his day, vast New England factories employed thousands.

Before 1838, he notes, most movements were wood; after it, metal ruled. Jerome tells of swindles, bad company, and his own hard trials. P T Barnum's part in the Yankee clock business earns its own billing. Makers and local readers get a pioneer's blunt, first-hand trade memoir.
narrative-of-a-mission-to-central-africa:
James Richardson led a British mission into Central Africa in 1850 and 1851. Her Majesty's Government ordered and paid for the trip. Richardson had written Travels in the Great Desert of Sahara. Chapman and Hall issued this account in London in 1853.

Richardson died on the journey and left a vast journal behind. His editor shaped eight small, close-written volumes into two books. Dispatches and loose memos filled out the record. The mission crossed the Sahara toward the great lakes and Sudan. Its reports opened Central Africa to British trade and science, at the cost of its leader's life.
nasa-tm-19680026299-cylindrical-electros:
J. A. Findlay and L. H. Brace of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this July 1968 preprint, X-623-68-281, on cylindrical electrostatic probes flown on two satellites. Alouette II and Explorer 31 carried identical probe sensors into the ionosphere. Flying the same instrument on both craft gave scientists a common yardstick for comparing direct measurements between missions.

The report explains the probe theory, the sensors and electronics, and how electron temperature and density are read. Satellite differences still changed data formats and experiment voltages, the authors note. On Alouette II, the topside sounder interfered strongly with probe data. Processing that data proved difficult, they add, though not impossible.
podcast-dannyjones-ABAvPuhu9yE:
Historian Richard Dolan built his reputation on books about UFO secrecy and a possible breakaway civilization. With Danny Jones, he turns from the sky to the sea. He presents what he calls the best evidence that unknown intelligences live deep under the oceans. It is a realm he dubs an underwater Area 51.

Dolan reviews sightings of objects entering and leaving the water at impossible speeds, many from military witnesses. The ocean is the least observed part of the planet, and his argument leans on that darkness. The claims are Dolan's, offered in his measured style, and they remain unproven. Listeners who follow his work get his full underwater case in one sitting, argued by the field's best-known historian rather than its loudest voices.
podcast-joerogan-3eZnbWTb1YE:
Dakota Meyer, a Marine veteran and Medal of Honor recipient, tells Rogan about turning to ibogaine therapy for PTSD. In a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, Meyer speaks as a man who tried standard care first and kept looking when it fell short.

He describes the treatment itself, a strong psychedelic given in a clinic setting, and the shift he felt afterward. Rogan asks what the nightmares and anger were like before, and what changed after. The segment adds a first-hand voice to the wider debate over psychedelic care for veterans who carry war home with them.
the-romany-rye:
Transcribed from the 1907 J. M. Dent edition, The Romany Rye opens with a chapter headed by the making of a linch-pin, a sound sleeper, breakfast, and a postillion's departure. No author's name is printed in the pages shown.

The narrator wakes at daybreak in a dingle, lights his forge, and fashions a replacement linch-pin for a chaise wheel, copying the pin from the companion wheel. Belle watches near the forge while the postillion sleeps so soundly in the tent that the narrator jokes he must descend from one of the seven sleepers. Fitted and polished, the new pin lets them put the wheel back on.
travels-in-the-united-states-of-america-:
William Priest, a theatre musician from Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Boston, published his American travels at London in 1802. The title page dates his stay from 1793 to 1797. His journals of two Atlantic crossings form part of the book.

Priest's preface admits he wrote the account for friends after coming home in 1797. Only their urging, pressed for three months, brought it to print. He credits extracts from Jefferson, Belknap, and other American writers for much of its value. Readers get a working musician's plain view of the young United States, offered without claims to fine writing.
